title: Events versus public delegates
hook: A long-lived SQS consumer that exposes a public Action field will leak every pipeline that subscribed once — and any code can null the field and drop production handlers.

sections.heading: Publisher, subscriber, and the event keyword
sections.prose: Events let a publisher notify subscribers that something happened. The publisher decides when to raise; subscribers decide what to do. An event with no subscribers is a no-op. Multiple subscribers are invoked synchronously in subscription order. The .NET pattern is EventHandler or EventHandler<TEventArgs> with a sender and args. C# 14 also allows partial events: one defining field-like declaration and one implementing declaration that supplies add and remove.

snippets.label: Field-like event versus a public delegate field
snippets.explanation: Outside the declaring class, MessageReceived supports only += and -=. UnsafeHook can be replaced with null by any assembler of the type, wiping metrics and ack paths together.

sections.heading: Unsubscribe or leak
sections.prose: The publisher’s invocation list holds the subscriber’s delegate, which holds the subscriber instance. A process-wide SQS or RabbitMQ host lives for the lifetime of the worker. A scoped per-message processor that += MessageReceived and never -= stays rooted until the host dies. Unsubscribe in Dispose, use a short-lived local function that you remove after the batch, or avoid events and pass an interface into the consumer. Custom add/remove accessors exist when you need synchronization or weak references; they must stay paired with -=.

snippets.label: Subscribe for a batch, then detach
snippets.explanation: The handler is a named method group (or a stored delegate). Unsubscribing a fresh lambda with the same shape does nothing — it is a different instance.

interviewTakeaways: event restricts callers to += and -=; only the declaring type raises and assigns.
Handlers run synchronously; isolate exceptions with GetInvocationList if needed.
Leaks: long-lived publisher + short-lived subscriber without -=.
You must -= the same delegate instance you +=; a new lambda will not detach.
commonPitfalls: Using a public delegate field as an 'event'.
Unsubscribing with a newly allocated lambda.
Raising events from a background thread without documenting reentrancy.

jsTsCorrelations.note: Browser events require the same function reference to remove, exactly like C# -=. JS does not stop you from replacing onclick entirely; C# event does.
addEventListener/removeEventListener is subscribe/unsubscribe. C# events hide the delegate invocation list.
